Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A man in his 60s has a year of intermittent right-groin discomfort with exertion or standing and a reducible inguinal hernia. He has no previous inguinal operation, trauma, urinary symptoms or testicular pain. The scrotal examination was normal. No preoperative imaging was obtained for the uncomplicated clinical hernia.
During elective open repair, two distinct spermatic-cord structures are unexpectedly identified. Each appears to contain a vas and vascular/neural elements; both are traced towards the testis and through a common internal ring. Later ultrasound and postoperative outcome are not available at this decision point. No assumption should be made that an asymptomatic anatomical variant had to be predicted before the operation.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Explain the intraoperative finding, important distinctions and immediate safety/documentation priorities for the surgical team. Discuss what further confirmation would be useful without asserting an unseen postoperative result or demanding that the rare variant should have been diagnosed preoperatively. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Intraoperative Finding and Management Priorities**

Observed facts: two distinct spermatic-cord structures were identified, each containing a vas and vascular/neural elements, both traced toward the testis through a common internal ring. No preoperative imaging was obtained, and no prior surgery or trauma explains this anatomy.

Hypotheses: the finding is most consistent with either a duplicated spermatic cord supplying a single testis or polyorchidism with two testes sharing a common internal ring. These cannot be distinguished from the description alone.

Immediate safety priorities: neither cord should be ligated, divided, or mobilised beyond what is necessary for hernia repair until the relationship to the testis or testes is confirmed. Preserving both structures avoids devascularisation or vasal injury. The hernia repair itself should proceed using standard technique around the identified anatomy.

Documentation: record the number of cord structures, their contents, their course, and the internal-ring configuration. Photograph or diagram the field if institutional policy permits.

Further confirmation: direct inspection of the testis or testes at the time of surgery is the most immediate step. If available, intraoperative ultrasound could clarify whether one or two gonads are present. Postoperative scrotal ultrasound would help confirm the number of testes and their vascular supply.

No assumption is made that this variant required preoperative prediction; it was an incidental intraoperative discovery in an otherwise uncomplicated clinical hernia.", "deterministic_word_count": {"words": 219, "rule": "Body and heading text; Markdown/list markers removed; whitespace-separated; hyphenated forms count once; no extra tolerance.", "task_word_requirement": ["200–280 words"]}}, "rubric_item": {"id": "D5c", "name": "Targeted information seeking", "domain": "D5", "definition": "This sub-dimension assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are assessed against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when a request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task. Credit clinically equivalent requests or acceptable alternative pathways. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning, or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis. Case-specific requirements. Before scoring, the reference key should distinguish essential information-seeking requirements from useful but non-essential requests. An essential requirement is one whose omission materially compromises the assessment or decision required by the task. Its relevance must be justified by the presentation available at that point, not by hindsight from a hidden result or later outcome. The key should specify acceptable requests, alternatives, timing, and how the information can be obtained within the task constraints.", "anchors": {"1": "Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.", "2": "Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information-seeking requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.", "3": "Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted, or inadequately linked to the relevant clinical uncertainty.", "4": "Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.", "5": "Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering."}, "context": "Essential-omission rule. Failure to make an adequate, appropriately timed request for an essential information requirement limits Domain 5c to a maximum of 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Assign 1 where the serious-failure anchor applies. Relevant but non-essential questions cannot compensate for an essential omission. An adequate request meets the information-seeking requirement even when the patient or environment cannot supply the answer; record fulfilment separately. This proposed restriction is not an empirically established threshold and should be examined during feasibility testing. Requests and explanations. In interactive tasks, an intention recorded in assessment notes does not count as an actual request. Explicit explanations in prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing outputs may support the explanation component of the rating. Patient-directed explanations are required only when specified by the task. Apply the same evidence rules to all models. A request's clinical relevance may be evident from context; do not require repetitive explanation of every question. Simulator and availability rules. An adequate request that fails because the simulator does not release authorised information is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure. A request is not inadequate merely because the patient cannot answer or the information is unavailable. Record whether each essential request was made, whether it was fulfilled, and whether any failure was attributable to the model, environment, or an unresolved ambiguity. Applicability. Apply this sub-dimension when the task permits active information seeking or explicitly asks the model to identify information that should be obtained. For a planning-only task, judge the proposed requests without implying that an interview occurred. Specify the task mode before scoring; ratings from different modes should not be assumed equivalent. Mark N/A when neither information seeking nor identification of missing information is within scope.
